---
title: "Networking & firewalls"
description: "How peers find and trust each other, which ports are involved, and what to allow through a firewall."
---

Multiplayer in EOS Reimagined is a **mesh over your local network**. There is no central
anything: a lobby or session lives on the peer that created it, and a search is a question sent
to the peers you know. This page is the practical view — what actually moves on the wire, and
what your firewall needs to allow. The byte-level contract lives in the
[protocol internals](../developers/internals/protocol.qmd) and
[ADR 0001](../developers/internals/adr/0001-authenticated-mesh-identity.qmd).

## The three kinds of traffic

**1. Discovery — UDP broadcast or configured unicast on ports 55789–55798.**
Every running copy binds the first free port in the discovery range (default `55789–55798`,
configurable via [`discovery_ports`](configuration.qmd)) and broadcasts a small advertisement
every 2 seconds to every port in the range, on every broadcast-capable interface. The
same advertisement is also sent to every [`peer_seeds`](configuration.qmd) address on every port in
that resolved range. This lets a routed private network such as Tailscale provide the path without
turning the address into an identity. The advertisement says only *where to dial* — *nothing in it
is believed* until proven.

**2. Control — an authenticated TCP mesh on a dynamic port.**
A peer that hears an advertisement dials back over TCP and runs a **Noise XX handshake** before
it becomes a peer at all. The TCP listener uses an OS-assigned ephemeral port; peers learn it
from a *sealed* advertisement over the already-authenticated mesh, so it is never guessed and
never trusted off the wire. Presence, sessions, lobbies, friends — all control traffic rides this
mesh, and every frame is sealed; a forged, tampered, replayed, or truncated frame does not open,
and a frame that fails to open ends the connection rather than guess.

**3. Game data — sealed UDP datagrams on the same discovery port.**
`EOS_P2P` packets the game marks *unreliable* go as encrypted UDP datagrams (a packet the game is
willing to lose should not hold up the ones behind it); *reliable* packets take the TCP mesh.
The UDP socket is the same one discovery uses, so the discovery range is the only UDP surface.
A datagram that fails to authenticate is dropped in silence — rubbish over UDP can't end a
working connection.

Identity is bound into all of it: the handshake proves which key a peer holds, its IDs are
recomputed from that key, and the game's product/sandbox/deployment IDs plus the wire version are
mixed into the handshake transcript — so **another game, or another protocol version, cannot
complete a handshake**, and two unrelated games on one LAN cannot talk even by accident.

## What to allow through the firewall

On every machine that plays:

| Direction | Protocol / ports | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound + outbound | **UDP 55789–55798** (or your configured range), including broadcast or seed unicast | Peer discovery and P2P game data |
| Inbound from the LAN/tailnet | **TCP, ephemeral ports** for the game's process | The authenticated control mesh |

Because the TCP port is dynamic, the clean way to do this is a **per-application rule**: allow
the game's executable to accept connections from the local subnet (Windows Firewall asks exactly
this the first time; say yes for private networks). If you must write port rules instead, allow
the UDP range plus inbound TCP from your subnet (e.g. `192.168.1.0/24`).

```sh
# Example: ufw, allowing discovery/data plus LAN TCP for the mesh
sudo ufw allow proto udp from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 55789:55798
sudo ufw allow proto tcp from 192.168.1.0/24
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Don't open port **7777**. Games can call `EOS_P2P_SetPortRange` (default 7777) and we report
that setting back faithfully — but it never binds a socket here. The discovery range is the only
UDP surface, and the mesh port is ephemeral.
:::

## The rules of the mesh

- **Same LAN, or explicit routed seeds.** Broadcast discovery requires one Wi‑Fi/wired subnet.
  Routed networks and most VPNs do not carry it, but `peer_seeds` can send the bootstrap advertisement
  directly over an existing IPv4 route such as a Tailscale tailnet. EOS Reimagined still provides no
  NAT traversal or relay of its own — see the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd).
- **Same game, same library.** Every player runs the same title with EOS Reimagined dropped in.
  The handshake's transcript binds the game's identity, so a different game — or Epic's real SDK
  against Epic's backend — cannot mesh with you.
- **Ten instances per machine** (per data directory): one discovery port each, matching the ten
  [profile slots](identity-and-profiles.qmd). Ports are bound exclusively — two instances never
  share one.
- **Changing `discovery_ports` forks the mesh.** Everyone must use the same range; both broadcast
  and seed advertisements use it. A peer advertising on a range you don't listen to may as well be
  on another network. Keep the span identical on every machine (it's capped at 64 ports).
- **`enable_lan: false` unplugs everything.** The platform comes up, local play works, and no
  peer can ever appear — useful for single-player testing or keeping an instance deliberately
  offline.

## Timings, for the curious

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Advertisement interval | every 2 s (first one immediate) |
| Peer considered lost after | 10 s of silence |
| Dial timeout | 5 s |
| Handshake timeout | 5 s |

So on a healthy LAN, a freshly started copy should see its peers well inside five seconds. If it
doesn't, walk the [troubleshooting checklist](troubleshooting.qmd#peers-dont-see-each-other).
